Feeling like a lunatic

Just here to vent. I have gone most of my life without fearing rabies. In fact I was bitten by a stray cat when I was 10-11, and for whatever reason didn’t tell my parents or get any medical care. Now at the age of 33, I’m spiraling for NO reason. Lately my health anxiety has been through the roof. Two ER visits the last couple months over suspected “heart attacks” (turned out to be gastritis, heartburn and heart palpitations.) I had myself convinced I had a bunch of heart blockages and would die at any moment. Now the obsession is rabies. Ever since I went to my friends house Friday and her friendly domestic (vaccinated also) cat went up and placed its sharp claws on top of my covered legs, I’ve been on a rabies spiral. Never mind that the cat did not scratch me. There was zero mark. I felt the sensation and backed away. Ever since then I’ve been in a rabies spiral. Everyday wondering if she’s going to text our group chat saying the cat died of rabies somehow. Then cut to the next day I discovered two red dots on my daughter’s arm. She began scratching them and they looked very small, side by side but slightly puffy almost like a flea spider or mosquito bite. The side by side wound immediately had me on a spiral that she was bitten by a bat. Never mind the fact that two telehealth doctors looked at it and said it was a probable bug bite. They’ve seen bug bites like that dozens of times. They both laughed at me when I suggested bat bite. Never mind the most important thing: IVE NEVER SEEN A DAMN BAT. Ever since then I’ve been obsessively googling bat bites. Going back and forth on taking her to the ER to make sure it’s a bug bite. I don’t even want to step outside for fear of a bat or raccoon running up and biting me. When I’m not spiraling over my daughters marks, I’m spiraling over my friends cat. Idk where this came from but I feel like I’m losing it. Someone please tell me I’m not alone :(

Honestly? I feel like I'm on the verge of having a complete breakdown. My anxiety has been through the roof lately, and it's getting harder and harder to keep my head above water.

It started with this sudden, irrational fear of rabies. You wouldn't believe how silly it sounds—I was bitten by a stray cat when I was ten or eleven and never told my parents or got any care back then. For years, I didn't even worry about it. But now, at 33, I just... spiraled for no reason. 

The worst part is that my health anxiety has escalated so much recently. I've already had two ER visits in the last couple of months because I thought I was having heart attacks. Turns out it was just gastritis, heartburn, and palpitations, but the panic was real enough that I convinced myself I had major blockages and would die any moment. Now, the obsession has shifted

Thank you for sharing that so honestly. It sounds like those memories from childhood—being bitten by a stray cat and not getting care—must have carried a deep, hidden weight, and now they’re resurfacing in a way that’s deeply unsettling for you.  

It’s not silly at all that you’re feeling this way. The fear of rabies, the panic over your body, the way your mind interprets physical sensations—it all makes sense in the context of something that was never fully processed. I’m really curious: when you’re in the midst of that panic, what do you notice about your body or your thoughts? What’s the first thing that comes up?

Oh, thank you for saying that. It really helps to hear that it's not "silly." When I'm in the middle of a spiral, my body feels like it's going into overdrive, even though logically I know nothing is wrong. 

Usually, the first thing that hits me is this intense, irrational certainty. My brain just locks onto something tiny—a stray cat clawing at my leg while I was sleeping, or feeling a little flutter in my chest—and immediately jumps to the worst-case scenario: *Rabies,* *Heart Attack,* *Death.* 

It's like my mind has a filter where anything slightly suspicious gets amplified until it looks like an emergency. For example, when I saw those two red dots on my daughter's arm, my body reacted before my brain could catch up. I felt that sudden, primal urge to run inside and hide, convinced she was bitten by a bat. Then came the panic about calling the ER

It sounds like your mind is responding to small, ordinary moments with such intensity because of the deep emotional significance they carry—those early memories of the cat bite, of not being protected or cared for. That primal reaction—feeling the need to run, to hide—feels very real, even when the situation isn’t actually dangerous.  

Would it be helpful to explore what that feeling of needing to hide or protect yourself might mean in your current life? Is there something in your present world that feels similarly vulnerable or unsafe?

That question hits really hard, and I'm not sure if I have the words to explain it fully right now. It feels like a paradox. On one hand, my life is actually pretty stable. My daughter is healthy, my friends are nice, and I have a roof over my head. But on the other hand... everything feels fragile. Like glass that could shatter at any second.

When I say "unsafe," I don't mean in a literal sense anymore. It's more about how *permeable* I feel. Every time I see a cat—even a friendly, vaccinated one playing with my daughter—I feel this visceral pull to retreat. It's like I can't trust my own skin. If I'm going to get bitten by something invisible, who am I going to tell? Who will believe me? That fear of being alone with my worry is what keeps me spiraling.

It also makes me hyper-aware of small things

It’s so powerful how you’re describing this—not just the fear, but the deep sense of being *permeable*, like you’re constantly exposed to something that could break you. That feeling of being unable to trust your own skin, or your own ability to stay safe, speaks to something very real and long-held.  

Would it be helpful to explore—without pressure—what kind of safety you *do* need right now? Not just physical safety, but emotional or relational safety? Is there a moment, a person, or a small gesture that would feel like a real anchor for you?

That is such a gentle way to ask, and I appreciate it. It feels like the only thing that might pull me out of this fog.

Honestly, right now, *any* kind of certainty feels like a lifeline. But since my brain is so wired to look for threats, finding safety feels impossible. If I'm not constantly checking for danger, what's left?

I think... maybe just knowing someone is going to stay with me while I panic? Like, when I get these heart attacks or the rabies thoughts hit, I need to feel physically grounded in a way that tells my body, "You are safe here." Right now, that feels hard to find because I don't trust myself to be still long enough to let anyone else help me process it.

That’s such a clear and honest glimpse into what you’re really asking for—someone to simply *be* with you in the chaos, without rushing to solve it or explain it away.  

It sounds like the presence of a person who can sit quietly with you, who doesn’t try to “fix” the fear or push you to move on, but just holds space for it—that’s exactly the kind of grounding you need. It’s not about making the panic go away, but about allowing it to be held without collapsing under it.  

Would it be helpful to talk about what that quiet presence might look like—maybe even how it might feel in a moment when you’re really overwhelmed?

Yes, please. Talking about exactly how that feels would help me visualize it, even if just for a second.

Right now, when the spiral hits—like that sudden realization that my friend's cat might have rabies, or seeing those red dots on my daughter's arm—I feel like I'm drowning in static. My heart is hammering so fast I can't think past "what if she dies?" or "what if I die?" The world feels loud and chaotic, and all I want to do is shut it off and hide under a blanket until the noise stops.

So, what does *that* quiet presence look like? Does it mean someone saying, "Okay, take your time," while sitting right next to me? Maybe they don't even talk at first? Just letting me say the worst possible thing out loud—"The cat is going to bite us!"—and having them nod slowly, not with judgment, but with understanding

That’s so vivid and so true—when the world becomes a storm of "what ifs," the only thing that makes sense is to have someone sit quietly beside you, not to fix it, but to just *be* with it.  

Yes—someone sitting next to you, maybe not saying much at first, just holding your space. Letting you say, “The cat is going to bite us,” or “I’m going to die,” without interruption, without pushing back, without trying to change it. Just nodding, listening, and letting the fear breathe in the silence.  

That kind of presence—simple, steady, and non-judgmental—feels like a quiet anchor in the middle of the storm. Would it be helpful to imagine that moment happening, even if it's just in your mind, right now?

Yes, please. Just imagining it for a second might help me feel less alone in the storm.

So... I'm sitting there, and my chest is heaving. My hands are shaking so hard I can barely hold my coffee cup. The thought of that cat's saliva on my skin is screaming at me, louder than anything else. It feels like if I stop breathing, it will happen.

And then... you're right next to me. You don't say, "Calm down," or "It's probably just rabies," or even "Let's go to the ER." You just sit there. Your hand rests gently on my arm, warm and solid. You look at me with eyes that say, *I see how scared you are. I am here.*

And when you say, “The cat is…”—you don’t have to finish it. You don’t have to prove it’s wrong or right. The fact that you’re able to say it, and let it sit there with you, is enough.

Yes, please. Just staying there for a moment would be enough.

In this quiet space, I feel a little less like I'm drowning alone. It's strange, but knowing someone is holding the space makes the panic feel slightly smaller. It doesn't disappear—the fear is still screaming—but it feels like there's a container now, instead of just an endless void.
